utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. PRESIDING OFFICER: We're going to start now. Mr. Sehapovic, could you please stand and read -- Are the interpreters ready? Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes. PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Sehapovic, could you please stand and read the text on the pink sheet of paper in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. PRESIDING OFFICER: Microphone. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There is no sound over here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear me? Can you hear me now? Can you hear me? No? My mike is on. PRESIDING OFFICER: Everything okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation] PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Lukic, we have no interpretation at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation] Is it all right now? Okay? Can we start now? Examined by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Sehapovic.

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would just like to remind you to speak slowly and wait for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We have a problem. Will you wait a bit, please? Can you hear this microphone? This microphone is working? And this one? Can you hear me now? Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we continue?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us slowly your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Ahmet Sehapovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ahmet, please slow down. Do you have any nickname that people know you by in Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the answer because of the overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since when have you been living in Samac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please repeat your nickname, but slowly.

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Cifun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us: When were you born? In what year?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Month and date?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: The 8th of December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are you by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are your parents by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: They are Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your marital status?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: I was married. I have a daughter. She's in America now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did your daughter go to America?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us: Where were you working? Where were you employed until the beginning of the war? When I say "until the beginning of the war," I'm referring to the month of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: I worked at the utility company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the popular name of that enterprise?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: The 11th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it called Komunalac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you tell me also whether, before the war, during the war, or after the war, were you a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: No, no party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What work did you do in this utility company before the war?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: I worked on waste disposal and tended to the garden.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maintenance in the city?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, city maintenance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sehapovic, had you heard of the Cafe AS?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to ask you several questions about the Cafe AS. I'm interested in the period prior to the outbreak of the conflict, prior to the war. Did you frequent the Cafe AS before the war?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: I practically was a fixture, so to speak, at the Cafe AS. I was there at all times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go there every day?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was there every day, without fail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the atmosphere like in this cafe before the war? I'm interested in the year 1991 and the first month of 1992. Did you come to the AS every day then?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Describe it for us. What was it like?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Serbs, Croats, and Muslims came there. There was no problem whatsoever, at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this cafe working around the clock?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: It worked until midnight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the owner of the cafe then?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Miroslav Tadic was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it have its permanent customers?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did members of all the ethnicities come there on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They came all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us: In that period prior -- just prior to the outbreak of the war, did you also go to the other cafes in Samac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any cafes that you were not particularly fond of, that you didn't like to go to, where you had problems?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were some. There were some.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where didn't you go?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't go to Mola, the so-called inn Mola.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the owner of that cafe?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Ratif Atic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is what by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Also a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why didn't you go to that cafe?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't go there because the crowd that gathered there was somehow strong, stronger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "somehow stronger"?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what I mean is well-heeled, moneyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did members of all the three ethnicities go to that cafe?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who gathered in this cafe, exclusively?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Izet Izetbegovic came, Omer Nalic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was asking you about Mola. What crowd came to Mola?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: That's it. Kemal Bobic, Fitozovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us: Did any one of these well-known Muslims also come to the AS cafe?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you see in the AS?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Izet Izetbegovic, Omer Nalic, Fitozovic as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these people ever have any problems with the guests in the Cafe AS?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: No. In my view, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you heard of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know who was in the 4th Detachment, or rather, did you know some people who were members of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the headquarters of the 4th Detachment was before the war?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the Sit, the Mladost Sit building is?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any signs, any emblems, any Yugoslav emblems, before the war on that building that you remember?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were they?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: They were the Yugoslav flag, and I cannot recall exactly what the other flag was at this point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there were two flags?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were two flags.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you ever seen any meetings being held at the AS, or that something unusual was going on relative to normal cafe life?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the people do in AS?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: They would gamble, they would shoot pool, they would sit there and have a couple of drinks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any excesses or any conflicts, any brawls in AS?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: This didn't happen there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Sehapovic: Did you see members of special units during the war in Samac, people who had come from Serbia, the so-called camouflaged people?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But were you aware that they were there in Samac? Did you hear about it?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard that they were there, but I didn't see them myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before the war, had you seen any people come to AS who were not from Samac municipality, people from outside, from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I shall deal with another subject. After the outbreak of the war, which is to say after the 17th of April, 1992, where were you working? Were you still working, and where were you working?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: I worked at the utility company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The enterprise where you had worked before?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you work at the utility company?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Twelve years and three or four months was the complete length of my service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the war started, how long did you remain working at this enterprise?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: For a month or two, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you receiving your salaries at the time?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were. Of course, there was a minimum wage.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will the witness please now be shown document 80A/1 ter, D80A/1 ter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, please look at the people on this list and tell me: Do you see your own name on this list?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know these people, the other people on the list?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: I know them all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This list has, so to speak, two parts: a first part, in which there were nine persons, and a second part, with three people. Is that not so? Look at these three people at the bottom: Safet Dubric, Sabahudin Coralic, and Ruzmir Mustafic. Did you work before the war with you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Safet Dubric did, and Sabahudin worked for a month in the lift [phoen].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they also receive their salaries?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were they actually added to your enterprise, or rather, when did they start working there?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall the exact time. I know that they came there to help out, as it were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mihajlo Sljokic, under number 2, and Kosta Mihaljcic, are they Serbs?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will the witness please be shown document D80B/1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see your name on this list?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the payroll for June 1992, so it is written here. Do you remember that in that month you also received a minimum wage?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: I did not get it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: Until what time did you remain working at the Komunalac, at the utility company? What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: I worked until June or July, I think -- May or June, sorry. And I don't --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what happened at that time? Did you get any summons to report anywhere?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I got a summons from Dzevad Celic; and not only I, but also some other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether this was a written call that you received and who signed it?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: It was signed by Bozo Ninkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you report to?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: To the pensioners' home, pensioners' club. I reported to Dzevad Celic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you working with a work detail or work platoon for a while?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: I worked with a work detail up to August, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What work did you do as part of this platoon?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we did various work, different work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, tell us one.

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, cleaning the streets. I was in charge of the machines, the lawn-mowing machines. Waste disposal, generally, was our job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given any salaries for that at that time?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: No, none.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened afterwards? Were you transferred to any other jobs? Were you called? Were you summoned to transfer to another service?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: I was called to transfer to the local community, to the local commune, as civil defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To whom did you report there?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: I reported to Ljubo Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am going to ask you about a couple of persons so that you would recall. When you came to the civil defence, was the civil defence office in the same building as the pensioners' club?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was, but not throughout that period. It was relocated later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Ljubo Vukovic. Do you remember whether you found there, in that period while you were working at the civil defence, Trivo Lukic?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the plumber, Ibrahim Karic?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, him I remember. There was also Mehmed Kurtic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember Isko, the driver?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are these Muslims?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Zeljko Volasevic perhaps among them? Do you remember him?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: He left. He left about that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the civil defence staff?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose it was Tadic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I saw him occasionally, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you doing in the civil defence? What kind of work?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: When we are told that a dead man has been brought, if he was killed, be he a Serb, a Muslim, or a Croat - it didn't make any difference - we would be called, those of us who would be working there, we would go there, bathe the dead man, and take care of everything. We would get a coffin and we would bury them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who would tell you that you had to go to the morgue?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Ljubo Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you started working on the preparation of bodies prior to funerals, were you in the civil defence all the time?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was offered to stay because few were willing to do this, so I stayed on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive a salary while you were doing that work?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did; not just me, but others as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive your salary in cash?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, cash, cash.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who gave you your salary?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Ljubo Vukovic did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the interpersonal relations in the staff in those days? Did you have any problems because you were a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: No, no problems whatsoever. Relations were first class.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the civil defence staff?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Until it was disbanded. Until it was disbanded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one other brief topic and that will bring us to the close. Were you engaged in the cutting of wood?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us what you did?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: I would load the timber and logs, and others would cut them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was this when you were loading the wood?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Niko Ivic was working on this, and Branko Djuric, Bacan Bogdanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did they cut the wood?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: In the woods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear them bringing timber from some abandoned houses in the village?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these unprocessed timber?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were logs, which earlier we used to cut with an electric saw. And now, where they would be taken, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the three persons that you mentioned cutting the wood, what ethnicity were they?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did they bring those logs to?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: To Buducnost. Now it's called Nova Forma.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do with the logs in Buducnost?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: We would have them sawed again with electric saws into smaller pieces. Then we would store them up. Now, where they would be taken, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were doing this while you were a member of the work platoon, were you not?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you later go to cut wood in the wood, in the forest?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this when you yourself went?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was sometime in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that ends my examination-in-chief. Madam Presiding Officer, rather. PRESIDING OFFICER: Cross-examination. Cross-examined by Mr. Re:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sehapovic, my name is David Re. I'm a Prosecutor. I'm going to ask you some questions about what you've just told us. You understand that? Before the war, that's before 1992, did you have a flat or a house in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: I had a flat which I hadn't received, really, yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you repeat your answer? Stop. Could you repeat --

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: I had a flat, but one that I still hadn't officially received.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just clarify something? Because I didn't quite hear your answer because of the interpretation. Before 1992, April -- Mr. Sehapovic, you must wait until I finish the question, listen to it, and answer the question I ask, please. Before April 1992, I want you to tell us: Did you own a flat or a house in Bosanski Samac? Just tell us again.

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: I did. A flat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you married?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I have one daughter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your wife: Muslim, Croat, or Serb?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your wife leave Bosanski Samac during the war?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: She didn't. My daughter did. My daughter went to America and my wife went to Austria before the war, because we were divorced -- after we divorced. We divorced a long time ago. The daughter stayed behind with me. She was 18 months old at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that during the war?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: No. My daughter was with me right up until 1995, during the war as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You had a flat you were living in in Bosanski Samac. Did other people move in with you during the war? You have to wait until the question finishes, it's translated, and then answer me. The question was: Did other people move in with you when you were living in Bosanski Samac in your flat during the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just clarify, to avoid any confusion? I would like the Prosecutor to ask the witness when he moved in. Then it will be clearer. "During the war" is a very broad concept, so I would like the question to clarify exactly the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992, 1993, 1994, or 1995, did anyone else move in with you in your flat where you were living in Bosanski Samac; and if so, who and when?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: In 1995 I was expelled, and at the beginning of 1996 a person came from Plehane. I don't know her name or last name. She stayed briefly. A second person came as some sort of boss. She stayed briefly too. And now there's a third person, who is still living in that flat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where are you living now?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm now living at my mother's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were expelled in 1995. Where were you expelled to, and why were you expelled?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Please don't answer this question. This question is absolutely outside the framework of the indictment, so I object to any questions being put or answered after 1993. It is quite outside the framework of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will press the question on the basis of its relevance to the witness's credibility and his experience in giving -- his experience and why he's giving testimony. The Trial Chamber will, of course, rule on whether the answer will be allowed into evidence later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question I asked you is: Why were you expelled in 1995, and where were you expelled to?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: They simply evicted me. They threw me out of my apartment; that's all. Refugees are coming. That was the sort of explanation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you expelled to?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: I went to my mother's, because I couldn't live in the street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't leave Bosanski Samac; you were evicted from your flat rather than expelled from the municipality. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: No one hurt me or expelled me in any way, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you worked on the work detail cleaning the streets, how many other people worked on that particular detail with you? Just the number, please.

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: It depends where people were assigned to. There would be three of us, five of us. It depended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the ethnicity of the people you were working with on the work detail cleaning the streets?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: There was a Serb working with me as well, a Serb too. Others were Muslims. Three, four, or five of us, as they would determine over there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were also working, you told us, on burying people of all ethnicities. When you buried people of any ethnicity - Muslim, Croat, or Serb, that is, Catholic, Muslim, or Orthodox - were they given religious burials in accordance with the rites of their faith?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The family would come for them. We would prepare them and do our work, and then the family would take them away and bury them according to their particular rites.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Leaving bodies in the street would have been a health hazard to everyone, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So bodies had to be buried, regardless of ethnicity, and as soon as possible, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your work detail at cleaning the streets, you were on one detail. How many other details do you know of were there also working in Bosanski Samac at the time?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: There was only one work platoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were cutting wood, your work detail cutting wood, how many people worked with you on the wood-gathering detail?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: There were six of them loading the wood. One was driving. No, I'm sorry. There were seven. Two of us would cut, five would load.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the other people Muslim, Croat, or Serbs?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: All were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the driver of the truck a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was in charge of this detail?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: We would get calls to report to cut wood, and we would report to Bozo Ninkovic. He would be the one signing the call-up paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever -- did you ever do trench digging?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said -- was it -- you reported to Bozo Ninkovic for the details or the assignment? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: A courier would come to fetch us, and he would have these papers, these documents, signed by Bozo Ninkovic. He would come to fetch us and tell us to go to the local community, and that was all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the courier?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Skejic Suad was the courier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His ethnicity was what?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: He was also a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said -- I think your words were that you were a fixture at the Cafe AS. Was this during the war as well as before the war?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Cafe AS was operating for how long during the war?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it stopped working. It didn't work for about four to six months after the outbreak of the war, because there was a prohibition on alcohol, a general prohibition on alcohol use.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, was it business as usual at the Cafe AS?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did work later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Serving alcohol?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Not much. Very little.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sehapovic, you told Mr. Lukic before that you were not a member -- you had not been a member of a political party. Had you had any political involvement, like assisting a political party, before or during the war?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you vote in the referendum on independence for Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you vote in the municipal elections in October 1990?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't have much interest in politics or government; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not a politician in any sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you following what was happening at a local level with politics in 1991, 1992?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: How could I follow? There was no electricity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were elections in 1990 and Municipal Assembly was elected. Did you follow the events, that is, the different parties being elected to the municipal government and what was happening there? Did you follow that through the media before the war?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: I don't really follow these things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, is he a friend of yours?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the owner of the cafe, and as I was there non-stop; that's as far as it went. He's a professor and I am an ordinary manual worker. A teacher, rather. He's a teacher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Cafe AS, did it seem to you to be a good business, a profitable business?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat that, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From going to the Cafe AS every day, being a fixture there, did the Cafe AS seem to you to be a profitable business, a good business?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, they did make a good income before the war, but the war did its bit. Everything was over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Mr. Tadic would have been short of money during the war because his business wasn't working?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. The witness is asked to speculate. I think the question should be rephrased. Did Tadic tell him? Was he aware that Tadic was short of funds? Or something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of whether Mr. Tadic was short of money during the war because his profitable business was no longer operating?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't tell you anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that Mr. Tadic was the -- was in the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you wouldn't have known that he was the assistant commander for logistics in that detachment?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you wouldn't have known whether the customers at Cafe AS were members of the 4th Detachment either, would you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: I am unable to say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that [Microphone not activated]... Exchange Commission in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: There were stories, but that's all. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Mr. Zaric? Do you know Mr. Zaric, Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I do know Simo Zaric, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know he was the chief of national security service for Bosanski Samac in the war, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Dr. Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I know him as a doctor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know he was the president of the Crisis Staff, then the War Presidency, in Bosanski Samac, in 1992, 1993?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I have no further questions. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. Mr. Lukic. Re-examined by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, for a point of clarification. I think that the Prosecutor didn't understand your answer quite well. When I asked you in the examination-in-chief how often you went to the AS cafe, you said: I went so often that I was married to it. What did you really mean? Were you referring to a wedding or how close you were to the cafe? When you use that expression, what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it means that I was a regular customer, that I came there on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went so often as if you had been married to it - that is an expression used in our language, to avoid any confusion - that you didn't really get married in that cafe. The Prosecutor asked you about religious rites at funerals, and you answered that. But in that connection, when you were washing the bodies, did you make an effort, taking into consideration the ethnicity of those persons? How was the washing of the bodies organised?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Three of us did it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But was it the custom for the Muslims to wash Muslims, and Serbs to wash Serbs?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Tiko Tesic [phoen] work with you on those same assignments?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you know that he washed bodies too?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: He's a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecutor asked you whether you know anything about Tadic's financial status before the war and during the war. Do you know whether Tadic assisted people of all ethnicities during the war?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: I have living proof of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... it doesn't arise from cross-examination. It's a question which, if it should have been asked, should have been asked in examination-in-chief. I asked nothing about Mr. Tadic's assistance to people during the war. So my objection is noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will respond, and I will press on with my question, because I think it does arise from the cross-examination. The Prosecutor asked whether the witness knew that Tadic, during the war, was short of money, that is, he had less money than before the war. So my direct question to the witness, arising from the Prosecutor's question, is whether he's aware that with his money, Tadic had assisted people during the war.

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did, with his own money.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that he assisted Muslims living in Samac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. There were a couple of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object. That's cross-examination of a witness, not re-examination. Again -- two objections: (1) It doesn't arise; (2) it's leading; (3) it's cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will rephrase this question, but I still believe it does arise from the topic raised by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did Miroslav Tadic assist during the war, giving money to them?

utterances.speaker: AHMET SEHAPOVIC
utterances.text: He assisted Croats, Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. Mr. Sehapovic, this concludes your deposition today. You may go now. Thank you for coming. We'll have a ten-minute --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too. PRESIDING OFFICER: We'll have a ten-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- Break taken at 10.02 a.m.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: Good morning, Mr. Jekic. Could you please stand and read the pink sheet of paper in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. PRESIDING OFFICER: The Defence for Simo Zaric. Examined by Mr. Lazarevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. You can sit down now.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jekic, I'm Aleksandar Lazarevic, an attorney. We've already met. And on behalf of the Defence of Mr. Simo Zaric, I will be putting questions to you. I would like to ask you kindly to make a small pause after my question, before giving your answer, in order for everything to be recorded properly. Now, please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Milan Jekic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you were born and where?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: On the 4th of September, 1954, in the village of Batkusa, Bosanski Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, can you tell us: Where are you living now?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: I live in the same village of Batkusa nowadays, municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us now something regarding your education. Where did you complete your primary school, secondary school, and so on?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: I completed primary school in the village of Obudovac, Bosanski Samac municipality. I completed secondary school in Bosanski Samac and then faculty of mechanical engineering in Belgrade, and I have a degree, BS degree, from there. I'm a mechanical engineer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now tell us: Did you complete your military service in the Yugoslav People's Army; and if so, where and when?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: I completed my military service in 1980 and 1981, in Skopje, in Macedonia. I spent my entire 11 months of service there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During serving, while you did your military service, did you have a rank?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was a private; and upon leaving the army, I was given the rank of private first class.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Tell us: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: I'm married and I have three children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now tell us: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jekic, were you ever a member of a political party?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: I was never a member up until 1990, and then in 1990 I was a member for a brief period of time, up until 1992. During that time, I was a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you a member of any party, political party, nowadays?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: I have not been in any party since the 16th of October, 1992. I'm political inactive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understood you well, you spent some two years in the SDS, from 1990 to 1992, and then following that you were not a member of any party?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you now something regarding your career. What jobs did you have, what tasks did you have, up until the April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: You mean from the very beginning of my life? What period are you interested in?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the time you completed the university. Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I worked in the secondary school centre in Orasje, then I worked in the factory in Gradacac, then in the repair shop in Modrica, and then for one year in the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now tell me, please, regarding your jobs before the war broke out: You said that you worked in the Ministry of the Interior. Can you tell us which public security station and what were your duties there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: I worked in the public security station in Bosanski Samac starting in mid-May of 1991, up until the 9th of April, 1992. My duties were that of the commander of the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what was it that happened on the 9th of April, when you ceased working there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: On the 9th of April, the then chief of public security station, he, as chief, and I, as commander of the police station, had to resign in writing, at the request of the staff, people who were employed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the record, please, can you tell us the name of the then chief of the public security station?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. His name was Vinko Dragicevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please: What is the ethnicity of Mr. Vinko Dragicevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: He's a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, on the 7th of April, you and Mr. Dragicevic, so to speak, left your work with the police. Can you tell us who replaced you, or rather, who replaced Mr. Dragicevic and you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you that. I didn't know it at the time. Later on I heard that the acting chief of the public security station was Dragan Lukac, and I don't know who became the commander. This is all the information I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I will not insist on any further details. I believe we have enough supporting information. Sir, now I would like to turn to the events during the night between the 16th and 17th of April, 1992. It has been established here that that was the night when the hostilities broke out in Samac. Can you tell us: Where were you that night, the night between the 16th and 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: I was in my bedroom, in my own bed. I slept during that night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I omitted to ask you something, and I believe it's not too late to do it now. Were you perhaps a member of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: No, I was not a member of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you perhaps a member of some other detachment with the Yugoslav People's Army up until the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: In that period of time, from the 9th of April up until the 18th of April, I was not assigned or attached to anything. I was simply unassigned. I was a commander of the police station who had resigned, who was suspended, who had to resign, pursuant to the request of the staff members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We just needed to be more specific about that, to see whether you were a member of any military unit.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: No. I was not active. I have not a member of any military unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now tell us, please: On the 18th of April, what happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or rather -- I apologise. My colleague has just suggested something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened on the 17th of April with respect to you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: As far as the 17th of April is concerned, I was called by the chief of the public security station, Stevan Todorovic, who was appointed by I don't know whom in Bosanski Samac. He called me on the phone, at home, and he knew that there was a reserve police station in Obudovac, which neighbours my village of Batkusa, and he told me to go there and to organise within that station, and with that station's personnel, several checkpoints that were on the roads towards Orasje, Gradacac, and the other side. And following that, I was to bring to him 15 members of reserve police to Samac, or else he was going to send people in camouflage uniforms to bring me in. So I had no choice but to try to assemble 15 people out of the 40 reserve policemen. I managed to find 15 people. We got into three vehicles. And then sometime around noon on the 18th, we got into vehicles and went to Samac, using the marked roads, because all other roads leading to Samac were blocked. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just clarify. When you say "people in camouflage uniforms, multicoloured uniforms," who do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Well, they were wearing multicoloured camouflage uniforms. I don't know where they had come from. And this is what we called them: camouflage people. It wasn't until later that we learnt that there had been some members of special units wearing camouflage uniforms and performing certain tasks and activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Therefore, on the 18th you, as you explained to us, got to the public security station in Bosanski Samac. Now, can you tell us briefly: What did you find there when you got there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: I found a complete chaos there at the station, and I saw people in camouflage uniforms there. There were six people wearing police uniforms who had come from the reserve police station in Gornja Slatina, and I saw quite a number of those people, and there were no former members of the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you got there and you found things the way you just described them to us. Did you receive any tasks or orders from the chief? What was your task supposed to be there? What jobs were you supposed to perform?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: On that day, after my arrival, certain other people came who used to work at the police station. One of those people later became commander of the police station, and he was appointed by authorities; I don't know by whom exactly. I told you that I was commander up until the 9th of April, appointed by the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And after resigning, I went there, upon summons or a threat by the chief of the public security station, Stevan Todorovic, and I was told that I was to be a person in charge of records and assigning people there, because that was within the scope of authorities of commander of the police station, who was supposed to assign former police members to various assignments within the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us: Who was the commander of the public security station then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: It was Savo Cancarevic. As I told you, when I got to the station, there were just six policemen there, six reserve policemen at that, and the rest of them were people in camouflage uniform. And as the day went on, the station filled with people. While I was there, for some two months, the station grew to some 250 people, approximately. I'm not claiming that it was exactly 250, but approximately there were 250 people employed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jekic, I have to ask you to slow down a bit so that the interpreters can manage to complete interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us something -- or rather, tell us what you know regarding an event, and this has to do with finding certain documents within the public security station. What happened? When did it happen? What did you find? Where? And so on.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Upon a threat received by one of those camouflage people, and later on I learned that his name was Lugar, who came and drank and said to us: Fuck your mothers. I apologise for my language. Fuck your communist mothers. If I find anything red or communist here, I will shoot them. I tried to save my own skin and I tried to resolve this in a normal manner, so to speak. And in the office of the former deputy commander of police station -- my office was in complete chaos and it was all wrecked, and I had to go into this other office, and I went through some documents, through some papers. And in order not to throw away things that did not have to do with communists but had to do with our profession and could potentially be important, this is what I left, and everything else that fell under the threat of Lugar I threw away. I threw it into a pile, and later on that was taken out. And while going through those documents one by one, I found some documentation of the SDA military organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Thank you. Now let me just clarify this by putting additional questions to you. So tell us first: What was the office in which you found this? We have had evidence here before this Trial Chamber and we know what the building looks like, so everybody is familiar with it. Just tell me, please: Was it on the ground floor or on the first floor?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: It was on the ground floor, and upon entering from Samac, one would face the windows of that office, and the windows of that office faced the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you said that that was the office of the deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell us: Who was the deputy commander then, at the time, on the eve of the breakout of hostilities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you: During that period of time, at the level of the Ministry of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the reserve composition of the then police elevated so that the former police station in Samac was included into a larger system, and four reserve police stations were established. One of them was in Samac. So in that police -- reserve police station, the reserve commander became deputy commander of the active composition. That was Mr. Joljic, who was -- and the another one was Namik Suljic. Since Joljic, the commander of the reserve police station, due to emotional and psychological problems, one month prior to that, left his job, everything was assigned to Namik Suljic, and therefore, during the last month, that was his office, Namik Suljic's. PRESIDING OFFICER: [Previous translation continues]... and Mr. Jekic, could you please speak a bit more slowly, for the benefit of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Presiding Officer. I'll do my best. [Interpretation] All right. We will try.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jekic, what was important for us was to hear whose office was it. So the office in which you found those documents, was the office used by Namik Suljic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: During the last month before the outbreak of the war, the sole user of that office was Namik Suljic, and him alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell us, please: Where in the office did you find the file with those documents?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: I found it on a shelf, on top of that shelf. I told you, there was a pile of documents, because the documents were piling in my office. But this particular file with these documents I found on top of the shelf.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... could be shown document D25/4, ter version. And I have a hard copy here, because it has quite a number of pages. And with permission, I would like to show the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Madam Presiding Officer and counsel, for the record, the witness was asked the date in the beginning, and we still haven't received any information concerning the date of this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I will clarify this with the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jekic, before you take a look at this document, can you please tell us the date? When was it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly, but it was one or two days upon my arrival there, so it could have been the 19th or the 20th or the 21st, at the most. I've told you here and I solemnly declared that I would speak the truth, and this is exactly what I'm doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jekic. You will tell us everything you're able to recollect, to the best of your ability. Now, will you please take a look at this document. Now you've looked at the document, and tell us, please: Is this the document that you found in the file in Namik Suljic's office?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is that document; however, a map is missing. It was a map in three colours. I'm telling you now: I had no need, I had no intention to go into analysis of this document. I simply found this document, I saw it, I leafed through it, and I set it aside, and then at about 1.00 a.m. I turned it over to Stevan Todorovic. But I remember very well that there was a map here with three colours - red, green, and blue - depicting the territory of Samac, the town itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, would you please go with us carefully through the first three pages of this document.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first page, the upper-left corner. We will agree, naturally, that it says here the SDA, the Party of Democratic Action, Bosanski Samac. Is this the first page that you found at the police station?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, exactly this one, because I remember well that this was the military organisation of the SDA party, nothing else. I remember this very well, that's for sure, and I know very well that that same commander, that night, took a pencil and found the names of certain people and called them on the phone, and he -- I can't remember the names of those people now. I remember the face of one of them. I don't recall their names. But he called them and told them to come to the station, and they replied: Mr. Commander, the curfew is on. When Stevan Todorovic, commander of police station, a Serb, tells you to come, then you ought to come. And this is how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now please take a look at page 2.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take a look at the names and tell us whether this is the second page of the document that you had found.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Well, based on these names, I know that Sulejman Tihic was the assemblyman representing the SDA in the Municipal Assembly. I know that Izet Izetbegovic was the vice-president of the Executive Council of the Municipal Assembly. I'm not sure exactly, but I know that he was a member of municipal government. Alija Fitozovic is somebody whom I know as a person who exists, but I don't know him personally. I know Omer Nalic from the electric power company. I don't know Safet Hadzialijagic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. What I'm interested in is whether this is the second page of the document you had found.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you that I know for a fact that that was the military organisation of the SDA party. I didn't go into the document analysis itself. I know that there were names there, that assignments within units, and phone numbers. I didn't want to analyse whose names I hear, what kind of people these were. I found this document at about 10.00 p.m., and I turned it over after midnight, at 12.30, to the chief of the police station. Therefore, I can't tell you, now that 10 or 11 years have passed, any more. I know for a fact that this was the military organisation of the SDA party. I know that there were first names, last names, units, and telephone numbers contained in it. I know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now would you please take a look at another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: May the witness be shown document D26/4. I believe it's ID still.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Then -- yes. Well, I apologise in that case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, this is a brief document. It only has three pages. Is this also a document that you found on that particular occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you with certainty. I cannot claim with certainty. As I told you, I didn't go into any profound analysis. I remember that what I found was military documentation of the SDA. I remember that there were names there listed, telephone numbers, that there were organisational units, and I remember this particular map, because it was at the end of the file. I cannot claim with certainty about this particular document, not with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Our copy says D26/4 ID. They indicated it was -- counsel indicated it was an ID document. Do you have records of when this was admitted? Because there was a partial admission of documents. I know we objected to this one, and the ones we objected to did not come in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The other one, actually.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: If we are referring to D25/4, pages 1 to 3 remain ID. The others were admitted on the 3rd of July, 2002. If we are referring to Exhibit D26/4 and ter, these were tendered on the 31st of May and were admitted on the 3rd of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I will -- okay. Let me ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just another question, Mr. Jekic, regarding these documents: To the best of your recollection, was the name of Sulejman Tihic on these documents that you found?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Q.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Well, there is nothing else that I can say, as I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You've already said that you handed over these files to Mr. Todorovic and what ensued after that, as far as he was concerned. Now I'd like to ask you several questions regarding the functioning of the public security station and at the time while you were there. First of all, I'd like to know: The bringing in of persons to the station, who within the framework of the public security station could order that a person be brought in?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: First of all, I should like to tell you that the orders were exclusively given by the head of the police station and the commander of the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If I understood you correctly, it was the head of the police station and the commander of the police station who could order anyone's apprehension and their bringing in into the station.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: During my time, I did not receive a single order to bring anyone in to the station. These orders were not given through or to me. These orders were given directly to the policemen involved, not through their heads. We were four in the shifts, and none of us -- no orders, that is to say, were ever given through any of us commanders, but these orders were directly given to the policemen involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What I want to know is: Who is the person who issued the orders?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: It was the head of the police station and the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Madam Registrar and Madam Presiding Officer, if you look at the list or the summary of -- END OF RECORDING ... isolated incident relating to the seizure of those documents. As a result, I move to strike all of this testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, for my learned colleague, I don't believe that this is that important, because the witness was a member of the police. He was in the police station. This is nothing that we haven't heard yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, if it's not important, then we will proceed --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. Then I will proceed, and of course the Trial Chamber will decide. Yes. And furthermore, when we heard the testimony of Mr. Todorovic and some other members, it seems that this document was a basis for arresting -- [Microphone not activated] ... certain people, so this is why I asked about these questions, and this is ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I'd like to ask you two things, first of all about Mr. Zaric. Did you see him at the time at the police station, while you were there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: I saw Mr. Simo Zaric once, perhaps twice, over these couple of days, the first couple of days, and afterwards I never saw Mr. Zaric throughout the period during which I remained at the police station, because our ways part totally after that. I went to the trenches, to the front line, to my unit, and I don't know where Mr. Zaric went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And just one other question regarding Mr. Zaric. While you were still seeing him, while you still saw him, was he wearing a uniform, and what kind of a uniform was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Well, from this distance in time of 12 years, I cannot remember. Perhaps, as I told you, I saw him once or twice during these first days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what he was doing then there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the conclusion, please describe the circumstances under which you left the police.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Well, okay. Well, what was the then militia, the police. I wanted to leave immediately after -- 15 days after I had arrived, but the circumstances were such that it was impossible for one to leave the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, please tell me: Why did you want to leave? And then describe the rest.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: In principle, I was a professional policeman for a short period of time. I was a policeman for a year in that particular police station. However, I was not averse to learning this new trade, and I did my best to become a professional policeman. At the beginning of the war, in the terrors that reigned, being professional was something which was not good for one, so that these [indiscernible], especially in view of the fact that I was a shift leader there, a person who was in charge of the paperwork, of assigning people to their respective duties, I didn't like it. So after 15 days, I wanted to leave. I wanted to go back to my own village, to go to the army, join the army there, but I couldn't, because of Stevan Todorovic, because this person told me: Why do you want to go there to join the Chetnik dukes [phoen], and this and that. But this is not the way I viewed things. He needed someone to do the work. And this is how it went on, how it was. I tried for another four or five times, and for a while I maintained these records and duty roster. And at a certain point I heard screams across the street in the territory of Defence Staff, and I went there and looked and saw a group of policemen hitting and beating prisoners. So I walked up to them. I slapped one of the policemen in the face. He fell down on the floor. Then he took a rifle and he threw it at me, and he told me: Fuck your mother. You want me to kill you? And he told -- I told him: Yeah, shoot. And then he went away. On another occasion, I drew out my pistol at a member of the police who was also behaving in this indecent way, and I simply told the head, the chief, Stevan Todorovic: Now you shoot at me. I'm leaving. I'm going. I'm calling it quits. And I left the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. But just please tell me: When was it that you joined the military unit after leaving the police, and where did you remain until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: At the end of July, 24th, 25th, or 26th of July, I left the police station. I had a furlough, a vacation period. I reported to my parent unit in my village. I told them that I had left the police, as a conscientious citizen, as I always was, and am, and the commander of this company to which I was assigned told me to go home for ten days and rest. I stayed at home for ten days. On the 3rd of August I reported to the unit and I spent the whole period of the war in this unit, as a member of it, of I don't know which battalion of the Bosnian brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jekic. PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Weiner. Cross-examined by Mr. Weiner:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jekic. I'm Phil Weiner. I'm from the Prosecution. I'm going to ask you few questions. Do you understand? Okay? Now, let's go back to 1990, okay? You were a member of the SDS party, political party?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, as of -- I cannot remember. I cannot tell you exactly when the SDS was set up, but perhaps a month or a month and a half after its inception I became a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you actually -- your name was on the ballot. You were on the SDS ticket for the Municipal Assembly; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were on the same ticket with Dr. Blagoje Simic; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And both of you, you and the defendant Blagoje Simic, were elected?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Blagoje Simic and I, and I think - I cannot say exactly - at least another 13 counsellors to the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. A total of 15 SDS members were elected?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you whether it was exactly 15. You certainly have a better figure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And in that election, the HDZ got 17 votes, the most votes; and as a result, HDZ nominated Vinko Dragicevic to be the chief of the police, or the chief of the SUP. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were nominated to be a deputy by the SDS, as a result of that election, in the police station?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: No, not a deputy -- not his deputy. The structure of the police station was not as such that I should be his deputy. I was just a commander of the police station, which is one organisational unit within the public security station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right. I'm sorry. I had the wrong term. You were nominated to be a commander after that election; correct? In 1991 you became a commander of the police station?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not only I; there were three candidates of the SDS who were to undergo a certain procedure at the level of the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's correct. And when you became a police commander, at that time you were an engineer by profession; your background and training was as engineer. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Graduated engineer of mechanical engineering.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You weren't a trained police officer at that time. You hadn't had a career in law enforcement at that time. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: It is correct. No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "no," you mean you were not trained as a police officer, you had not had a career in law enforcement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Until that time, I had not been a professional policeman, but a professional mechanical engineer, and I worked in my profession, which is mechanical engineering.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you stayed in the police station until about 10 days, 14 days prior to the outbreak of war, when you left and went back to Batkusa, where you stayed home where you lived?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: I did not leave the station in that sense. I and Mr. Dragicevic, at the request of the staff, had to resign, in writing, as both the head and the commander of the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All I'm saying is: When you left the police station, you were still living in Batkusa and stayed at home in Batkusa, for approximately two weeks, 10 days to two weeks; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Batkusa is a small village in the municipality of Samac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Yes, a relatively small -- it's an average-size village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you aware while you were home in the village of Batkusa that around April 11th a group of these volunteers from Serbia, or the camouflage people, arrived by helicopter, 30 of them? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: I was not aware of it, but I had only heard about this, because I'm that kind of a person; I'm not very communicative. I didn't go to see or -- I rather heard some stories from women and men that there were some camouflaged people around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's continue on. You start working at the police station at approximately April 18th, and you stay through the middle part of the summer, correct, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Until sometime -- the 24th, the 25th, or the 26th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you worked under Stevan Todorovic, who was the police chief?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
