utterances.text: My superior before him was the commander of the police, Savo Cancarevic, and after him, Stevan Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you indicated when you first got there, on or about April 18th and through the 19th, it was chaos; isn't that correct? You described it in your direct examination as complete chaos.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there were people coming and going from the police station. There were JNA people, there were paramilitary or camouflaged people, there were all sorts of people in and out of the police station, isn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I object. This is not what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. I'm asking the question. I'm not saying that he stated that. I'm asking the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Weren't there people coming and going from the police station that were not regular police?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you: When I came to the station on the 18th, I found six reserve policemen there from the reserve police station, from Gornja Slatina, and I also found these men in camouflage uniforms, these multicoloured uniformed people, as well as Mr. Stevan Todorovic, the head of the station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the 19th, on the following day, people were still coming and going from that police station, and I assume on the 20th and 21st too.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Well, these camouflaged people were there. Theirs was the largest number in these first days in the police station. And as time went on, there were fewer of them and there were more of the regular police, because the normal establishment of the police was being manned by standard policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also at that same time, people were being arrested, houses were being searched. Over those first few days after the war began, people were being -- houses were being searched, people were being arrested, and they were being brought into the station and sent across to the TO; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Well, as I say, these first apprehensions of people, the bringing in of the people in the initial period was the work of these camouflaged men. And as time elapsed, the number increased of policemen, and it was then they who actually brought people in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. My question is: During these first few days, people were being arrested, houses were being searched? I'm not asking by whom, but just that people were being arrested, houses were being searched, prisoners were coming into the police station, going across to the TO. You were aware of that, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: No, not in the sense that I knew much about it. I know what happened on the 18th, when I arrived, that certain people had already been brought into custody. On the 18th there had been -- when I arrived there, I saw some people, a certain number of prisoners in the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking if you were involved in it or if you knew about it, but did you see it? Did you see over the next few days people being brought in to the police station as prisoners? That's all. You saw people on the 18th. Did you see people on the 19th and the 20th too, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Well, as I was saying, there were arrests on the 18th and 19th and 20th. I didn't count how many such cases there were. Some people were brought in for interrogation purposes and probably released to go home. Others were kept in the police station or, rather, in the TO staff building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during those first few days, you saw Stevan Todorovic in the police station, on the 18th, 19th, and 20th; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Stevan Todorovic was in the police station throughout that period, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also see Simo Zaric during those few days, first two or three or four days in the police station?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I object. This is a repetitive question. This is the same question that I asked the witness, and he has an answer. We have an answer for the record. Exactly the same question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's the entry question that I'm going to use to discuss what's going on. That's -- I want to enter into an area relating to Simo Zaric, so I should have the right to ask him if he saw Simo Zaric first. Otherwise he would be objecting that I haven't laid a proper foundation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, during those first few days, you also saw Simo Zaric in the police station?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Once, or maybe twice. From a distance of 12 years, I can't remember how many times I may have seen Simo Zaric. As I said, once or maybe twice, on the first or second day. I hope you understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sir, did you speak to Simo Zaric or did you just see him moving through the station on that date, or on those dates that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: I never had any close relationship with Simo Zaric in any sense of the word.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know what he was doing on those one or two occasions that you saw him at the police station, you don't know what his activities were; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: I have no idea what he was doing, why he came there. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know what, if any, conversations he was having with Stevan Todorovic or Savo Cancarevic during those days when you saw him at the station?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: I have no idea. I know nothing about those conversations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let us continue. Sir, did you ever, as a commander, appear before the Crisis Staff during the month of April 1992, either April or May, or at any time while you served as a commander of the police station?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: I don't know which Crisis Staff you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff of Bosanski Samac, the Serbian municipality of Bosanski Samac, which was chaired by the defendant Blagoje Simic. Did you ever appear before that Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you something: I don't know at all that that Crisis Staff existed. I knew so little about these things, and I was not much appreciated in the SDS, so I knew very little. I had no idea that such a Crisis Staff existed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you weren't aware that Stevan Todorovic was a member of the Crisis Staff and attending Crisis Staff meetings? Were you aware of that? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that Stevan Todorovic travelled to Belgrade in early May with Simo Zaric, Blagoje Simic, and Miroslav Tadic, in early May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, it has been uncontested in this case concerning a number of terrible things that occurred at the SUP and the TO, that people were beaten and tortured and there were sexual assaults, robberies, murders. You're aware of that? I'm not saying you were involved in any of that, but you're aware that these terrible things happened?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: As I didn't wish to get into conflict with myself, as you understand. My reasons for leaving the police station were things of that kind, because that was not the professional way to address problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you said, it wasn't being run professionally. But those terrible things were happening, and that's why you said it wasn't being run professionally; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: As I was saying, I couldn't understand that somebody would be doing something in a way that was not being done professionally, and as I couldn't join in acting professionally, I distanced myself from such behaviour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you're also aware that Stevan Todorovic, who was the chief, has admitted to committing a number of terrible crimes, including illegal arrests, detaining civilians in inhumane conditions, beatings, sexual assaults, murders, forcing persons to sign false confessions? Are you aware of that, that he's pled guilty and has admitted to that conduct at the SUP, the TO, and the primary and secondary schools? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of those facts, because no one told me about them. I don't listen to the media even, because my position towards such media is a negative one, so I'm not familiar with what Stevan Todorovic said, what he declared, or what he admitted to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, you had seen some unprofessional conduct, some terrible things happening. You knew the president of the SDS party was Blagoje Simic. Did you go to Blagoje Simic and say to him: Some terrible things are happening? Did you complain to him, Dr. Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're an intelligent man, you have a degree, you're a very bright man. You wouldn't -- you must have been appalled by what you were seeing. Did you complain to anyone? Were you able to complain to anyone about what you were seeing?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Five times I complained to Mr. Stevan Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to no avail?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you didn't complain to the Crisis Staff or Dr. Simic, who you were on the same ballot with?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: You are confusing some basic notions, Mr. Prosecutor. You are involving me in the pre-war Municipal Assembly of Bosanski Samac, and then in the Serbian Municipal Assembly that I had nothing to do with, you see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't complain to them. But let me ask you this, sir. You indicated that you didn't complain. You also indicated during your testimony that you left the SDS party in 1992, in October. You're nodding your head in the affirmative. Do you mean yes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that because you disagreed with some of their policies?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're aware that the leaders of the SDS, the national leaders at that time - Biljana Plavsic, Karadzic, Krajisnik - have all been indicted for war crimes and persecutions of the non-Serbs of Bosnia? You're aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: I heard about it over the media.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that you weren't in favour of the SDS policies of persecution of the non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Certainly I didn't agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you found those papers, anywhere from the 19th to the 21st of April, you found them in a pile, you gave them to Stevan Todorovic. Prior to giving them to Stevan Todorovic, did you make an inventory or summarise each page or make a copy for yourself, or did you just give them to Stevan Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: I simply gave them to Stevan Todorovic. But because I had no need to go into that. I was no longer a professional. You understand? I was not working for money any more. I was engaged under wartime conditions. So I found the document, saw that it has a certain validity, I forwarded it on to Mr. Stevan Todorovic, and that was all I had to do with that document, for good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than contacting people to come in whose names were listed on those papers, you don't know what Stevan Todorovic did with any of those papers, what his analysis was or what he in fact did with any of them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: I have no idea. I just know that that same evening, he took two men into custody by telephone, and nothing more about that document until I was called to testify in this case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: May I just have one second to confer?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Re-examined by Mr. Lazarevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I had intended not to ask any additional questions, but I do have one. Would you tell me, please: Did the SDS, at the local level - I'm talking about the level of Samac municipality - did it advocate certain programmes of division on ethnic basis?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: This is not cross-examination. That's a leading question. If you want to ask an open-ended question, you can, but that is a leading question and it's not permissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I will rephrase that. I will rephrase that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was phrased in such a way that it is not appropriate for this part of the examination. But as the Prosecutor has already asked you something, and this question arises from that question: What was the SDS programme at the local level, at the level of Samac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JEKIC
utterances.text: To tell you quite frankly, though I was a member of the SDS in those days, I was not in the higher-level echelons of the SDS to know these things. In any event, the relations were better with the HDZ and the SDA than with the SDP, the former League of Communists. I know that from the level of the Municipal Assembly. But what their further plans were, I don't know. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. Thank you for coming here today to give your deposition.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome. PRESIDING OFFICER: You are free to go now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: We're going to take the lunch break now, as I understand. You can only take the next witness after the lunch, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] PRESIDING OFFICER: Okay. Okay. Fine. Okay. So we'll have the next witness -- we'll have a ten-minute break and then the next witness. --- Break taken at 11.21 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: Good morning, Mr. Arandjic. Would you please stand and read the text on the pink sheet of paper in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. The Defence for Mr. Zaric. Examined by Mr. Lazarevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Good morning, Mr. Arandjic. On behalf of the Defence of Mr. Zaric, I will be conducting your examination-in-chief. For the record, could you give us your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: I can. My name is Stevan Arandjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. To cover your personal data quickly, and that was also the suggestion of the Trial Chamber before we arrived here, so I will put my questions in such a way that you can just answer them with a yes or no, so that we can save as much time as possible. Were you born in Gornja Slatina on January 1st, 1959?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is in Bosanski Samac municipality?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your ancestors have been living for centuries within the territory of Samac municipality?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me, please: Since when have you personally been living in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: I personally have been living in Bosanski Samac since the end of 1982.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are married and have a daughter?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me now, briefly, please, what your qualifications are, your educational background.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: I attended elementary school in Gornja Slatina, in a village of Bosanski Samac municipality, where I was born. I attended and graduated from secondary school in the municipality of Gradacac, which is to the south of Bosanski Samac. And upon graduation, I enrolled at the faculty of General People's Defence and Social Self-Protection in Sarajevo, which is a department of the faculty of political science. The courses lasted four years and I graduated in 1982, around April or May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you tell us, before the outbreak of hostilities, that is, before the 17th of April, 1992, where you were working and what your job was.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Prior to the beginning of these unfortunate events, I was working in the department of the Defence Ministry, called, before the war, the Municipal Secretariat for National Defence of Bosanski Samac, as a municipal inspector for the National Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us where you are working now?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: I'm still working now in the department of the Ministry of Defence of the Republika Srpska, for Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By ethnicity you're a Serb, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you now a few -- could you tell us a few words about your party affiliations. Were you a member of a party? Did you join any parties? What party are you a member of now, perhaps? A little bit about your political career, if we can call it that.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia ever since secondary school, that is, sometime in 1977, up until 1990, when the multiparty system was introduced in the former Yugoslavia, that is, in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. On that occasion, I joined the Alliance of Reformist Forces for Bosnia-Herzegovina, headed by Ante Markovic. After that, I was not involved in politics, and my professional duty today is incompatible with politics. As a person, too, I am apolitical now. I do not support being a member of any party. At least, those are my opinions today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Tell me now: Did you do your national service with the JNA, when, and did you have a rank?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: My four-year university course, including training for a reserve non-commissioned officer, so that as part of my education I also regulated the question of military service. And when I graduated, I acquired the rank of a non-commissioned officer, and of course in the reserve force over the years I was promoted to the rank of reserve second lieutenant, and that was the rank I held in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let me now move on to another topic, that is, the 4th Detachment. Can you tell me first whether you were a member of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you joined that detachment, what was your role in the detachment, and a few details about it.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the 4th Detachment, and as a reserve lieutenant, I was assigned to the position of an officer, that is, the commander of the 2nd Company of the 4th Detachment of the JNA. So I became a member of the detachment sometime around the beginning of 1992. I can't tell you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We won't insist, of course, but I would like to ask you: When you say you became a member of the 4th Detachment, tell us how you became a member. What was the procedure?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: I was a military conscript, and as such, I was given a wartime assignment and I was told which position I would hold in this military unit. It was not my choice; it was my duty which I had to fulfil and carry it out to the best of my abilities. Of course, the other citizens too of the municipality of Bosanski Samac could have voluntarily become members of the 4th Detachment, if they were not given such a wartime assignment, since the unit was in the process of being formed, while at the same time the nationalist parties were developing their paramilitary formations, so that every military conscript who felt that the values that needed to be defended through the 4th Detachment of the JNA joined that detachment voluntarily, so that the unit wasn't fully completed when the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You already said that the 4th Detachment was part of the JNA. Tell us: What was the next level of organisation above the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The 4th Detachment was an integral part of the 17th TG, or Tactical Group, which was being formed, and one of the detachments was this 4th Detachment, which consisted of the citizens of the town of Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: Regarding the command of the 4th Detachment, who was the commander and who was the deputy?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: The commander was a major in reserve, Radovan Antic, and his deputy was a reserve captain, Jovo Savic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know what positions were held in the 4th Detachment by Mr. Simo Zaric and Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Like any other detachment, this 4th Detachment also had a certain number of assistants, or rather, every commander had a certain number of assistants. So this commander too had a number of assistants, and Mr. Zaric was the assistant commander for security affairs in the detachment, whereas Mr. Miro, Miroslav Tadic, was also an assistant commander, but for logistic supplies for the unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the interest of better understanding of the whole story of the 4th Detachment, was this a unit stationed in the barracks, or how did it actually function?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: I've already told you that this was a unit that was just being formed, so that it was in the preparatory stages. It had its nucleus, and it was being reinforced with time and strengthened, but it didn't have its own barracks, it didn't lead the life of a military wartime unit, so that the members of the 4th Detachment, and members of other detachments too within the framework of the 17th Tactical Group, never gathered at one particular place to demonstrate their strength or their power or their physical integrity and wholeness. I think that many didn't even really know who the members were, except, of course, the officer staff and the command staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you: Were you issued a weapon in the 4th Detachment, and did the others have weapons?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Since the 4th Detachment was in the process of formation, I was issued an automatic rifle, in the unit command which was accommodated in the state-owned enterprise Sit, of Samac, in two offices, and that is why I swear I signed the receipt and took over the weapon, whereas a certain number of members were not armed, because the whole process had not been completed. It was still ongoing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We won't go any further into the details. We will have some other witnesses who will testify to that. Let me just ask you now to pass on to the night between the 16th and 17th of April, 1992. Could you tell us where you were on the evening of the 16th or the morning of the 17th.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you: I was performing my regular duties in the Municipal Secretariat for National Defence, as an inspector for National Defence, as I said, and on that day I returned home, as I had on all the previous days, not knowing what would happen. And of course, sometime after midnight, I was woken up by shooting in town, in the eastern part of the town. I could hear echoes of bursts of fire and individual shots, from infantry weapons, of course. This is the area known as Donja Mahala. The telephone lines were cut, and I was waiting to see what would happen, and expecting somebody to call me, to report for duty. Of course, it was highly risky to leave the house on your own initiative, and I waited until morning. And in the morning, the telephones started working again and I was called up to report to the command. This may have been around 8.00 in the morning. And I went out and reported for duty in the command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I just forgot to ask you something. I think I did put it to you, but I didn't get an answer. What was your actual position in the detachment?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: My position was the commander of the 2nd Company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: What does that mean in practice? How many men came under your command or did you have control of?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: My company was not fully formed. It should have numbered up to 120 men, but in fact, in my company, there were about 40 members, so that it was still in embryonic form.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you now continue where I interrupted you. You were called from the detachment's command and you went there. Tell us: When you arrived, what did you find there?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: I reported to the unit's command and I was informed about the latest development. I was tasked to try and rally members of my unit, calling them up by telephone, and a certain number of them did respond. This lasted a couple of hours. And as I was saying, out of those 40-odd members, quite a large number did not respond, either because they were simply unable to come, it was not possible to arrive, and also a number probably had left the town, maybe that very night. So that a small number responded, only some ten, perhaps, from my company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you gathered there at the command, and these ten or so members of your company. Were you issued an order; if so, from whom, and what was it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Well, since the situation in town was still raw, I was given an order to use my company, together with the 1st Company, to take position of defence along the embankment of the Bosna River, in the western part of Samac. So we were to take positions there in order to prevent possible incursion of Ustasha forces from Kura [phoen] village, which was separated only by Bosna River, and river at that time of year had a very low level. There is a small provisional bridge over the Bosna River, which was in use at the time, and it was held by Muslim and Croat extremists. Therefore, there was a possibility for some part of the forces to be transported into Samac through that bridge. Therefore, I tried to gain control over the bridge and the area of the bridge, and rather, to put it under the control of the 4th Detachment of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us: What time of the day was it when you went there?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: It was daytime. It could have been sometime around noon or 1.00 p.m. I'm not quite sure. I attempted, with a group of my company men, after sending other members to the embankment, I started with the first group towards the bridge, using local objects that were there in order to shelter us. We approached the bridge and the road that was parallel to the road that led over the bridge to the village of Prud, which is some hundred metres from the bridge itself. We came upon a group of two civilians, one of whom was armed with a rifle, with Kalashnikov rifle. The other one was not armed. And these two men controlled the access to the bridge from the direction from which we came, and they enabled an unhindered passage over the bridge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the record, can you just be more specific about the identity of these people?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: To my surprise, I learned my fellow citizens -- I recognised my fellow citizens, Ramusovic, Srna, Izet [as interpreted]. As I said, to my surprise, because his brothers were in the 4th Detachment with me, his three brothers. One of them was even wounded in town by Muslim and Croat extremists. And the other person was Safet Srna, a bit older than Izet, and he seemed to be drunk, Safet Srna. Naturally, they didn't notice us. They controlled the access to the bridge by moving in both directions and observing the access to the bridge from the direction from which we came from. I didn't have much time to think this through, nor did I have an opportunity to return, because, you see, there was an imminent danger of being noticed and eliminated by them. So I stood hidden behind a concrete fence next to the house, where people lived, obviously. He passed right by me, giving me an opportunity either to disarm him or eliminate him. Naturally, it didn't even occur to me to kill a person whom I knew and who was my fellow citizen and with whom, a month ago, I participated in helping a fellow citizen build a house. This is somebody who glorified Yugoslav People's Army, who criticised nationalists, and who advocated the values of the former socialist Yugoslavia, and by this I mean unity, brotherhood and unity, and so on. And then all of a sudden I saw that man in front of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us: Who are you referring to now?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: I am referring to Izet Ramusovic. Therefore, I was shocked. So I didn't have much time. All of this evolved in a few seconds. And I used the shelter behind that fence, behind that house, and yelled in a loud voice for him to throw away his weapon. To my surprise - and this is a small house that I'm talking about. It was some seven by six matters - and he started facing towards me with his weapon at shoulder height, and he lifted the -- or turned the barrel towards me, opening fire, but fortunately the bullet ricochetted off the house wall, and fragments of brick and facade ended up spraying on my face, forehead, neck, and so on. I returned fire. I opened a brief burst of fire, and at the height of his feet. I had no intention to kill him. I wanted to frighten him or perhaps wound him in lower legs. He shot out two more bursts in my direction and disabled my rifle for any further action. The front-end side and the backside were disabled on my rifle, and one bullet hit the barrel, so that my rifle was fully disabled. One bullet hit one of my fingers, grazed my fingers, and I wasn't even aware of that. My fellow soldiers were very frightened for me. They went pale when they saw me. However, I think it was fortunate that none of us was armed. He fled together with Srna Safet. Following that, very strong sniper fire ensued, which made it impossible for my group to proceed, and we returned to the place where we had started out from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now let me ask you this: Is there any doubt in your mind regarding the identity of the man who shot at you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: None whatsoever. As I've said to you, this is a person whom I knew personally, who was my fellow citizen, with whom I jointly participated in building my neighbour's house, right next to my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following that incident, you went to the command, as you told us. Did you speak to somebody regarding this incident? Did you report it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if so, whom did you report it to?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: I was provided medical assistance in the first building next to the command. I was given medical assistance. My face was cleaned and then my hand was bandaged. I established contact with commander and his deputy and informed them about the situation, about what had happened, also telling him about the identity of the persons that put up resistance to us. And I believed that my task was over and that it was now in the hands of the command, of the commander, and other organs of the unit, to see whether they wanted to undertake something else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they say that they wanted to undertake some other steps? Did they suggest anything to you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: You know what? Simo was present there, as was Radovan, and they were just as surprised and shocked as I was upon learning of the identity of this person, because, as I told you, his other three brothers were members of the detachment. So they told me: Thank God, Stevo, that you weren't wounded or killed. Then they cursed him and said: Well, just -- let's just leave -- let's just leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said "Simo" and "Radovan," can you please give us their last names.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Simo Zaric and Radovan Antic. They were the persons whom I informed about the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Madam Presiding Officer, I wonder if counsel for the defence could ascertain from the witness who the commander and the deputy were that he reported the incidents to, whether in fact they were Simo Zaric and Radovan Antic, or whether they -- the commander and deputy commander were two separate people. I'd just like to know to whom the reports were made, if that can be ascertained with absolute clarity. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe that -- yes, I believe that the witness already said that, but let's go through this again. I hope -- MR. DI FAZIO: I don't need it in chapter and verse; I just want to know if the commander and deputy commander --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I hope it won't affect my time for -- yeah. MR. DI FAZIO: I don't need it in chapter and verse; I just need to know whether the commander and deputy commander to whom this --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So please tell us, since we are now talking about deputy, assistant: Now, who exactly were the persons whom you informed about that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: As commander of the 2nd Company, I had an obligation to inform my detachment commander about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Reserve Major Radovan Antic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other individual?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: There in the command was also his deputy, Reserve Captain Jovo Savic, as was Simo Zaric, as assistant commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we're talking about three persons: Radovan Antic, Simo Zaric, and Jovo Savic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And I had a duty to report to the commander of the detachment about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. As I understood it, they told you to leave this aside, to disregard this.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what explanation did they give you for that? What did they say to you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Well, I've just told you, in a way, that his three brothers were members of the 4th Detachment of the JNA. They were not members of my company, but regardless of that, I knew, as they did, the commander or the deputy commander, about this fact, and they tried to soften this in order not to create a bad feeling within our unit. So they just wanted to cool this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you personally report this to anybody else, I mean the police?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Every learned of this incident, all members of the 4th Detachment and, naturally, other residents of Samac and members of the MUP. Therefore, not immediately, but after a month or so - I'm not quite sure whether it was 30 days or 45 days later - I was called to the police station to see Mr. Milos Savic in order to give a statement about this incident. I responded to this call and I described the incident as I just said to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the function of Milos Savic within the police?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: I believe that he was an investigative judge perhaps, or -- I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. But he was an investigative officer of MUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So you gave a statement to Milos Savic. Did something else happen regarding this wounding of yours, and what can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: As far as this incident is concerned, the following year, 1993, the military court in Bijeljina started proceedings against that man because there were some other events regarding that person, and all of that created the conditions for filing charges against Ramusovic. I was called to report to the military court in Bijeljina and give a statement, again pertaining to this incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now tell me this, please: You came to Bijeljina. Where did you go to, whom did you see, who was present, and so on?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: The proceedings were conducted by a judge of the military court. The defendant, or the suspect at the time, was defended by a major. He was an appointed counsel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me put a question regarding that. This gentleman, major, who you say was appointed as a counsel, was he present throughout the proceedings? Was he present when you gave your statement?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Not only he was present, but to my surprise, he put such uncomfortable questions, prying questions, to me that it made me feel quite uncomfortable here and there, and then after that I was told that he took advantage of all of legal provisions available to him in order to defend his client.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he deny your story? Did he try to challenge what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are now, naturally, referring to the court-appointed counsel for the accused.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times did you go to Bijeljina regarding this matter?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: I believe I went twice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as you were describing the trial to us, and you told us about the defence counsel, the prosecution, the military court, and so on: Was that on the first occasion or on the second occasion?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: It was on the second occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when was the first occasion when you went to the military court in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: The first time I went there, I gave a statement, and I believe that on that occasion, Ramusovic wasn't present, whereas on the second occasion, both Ramusovic on the major defending him were present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. On the second occasion when you were there, was there a judgement passed down? Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: I personally didn't know what the final outcome of the trial was. Yesterday I had occasion, while preparing for my testimony, to see that judgement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, you didn't know what the outcome was, outcome for Ramusovic? You didn't know that at the time?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: I learned it through the mass media. I learned when it was announced that he had been exchanged, and later on I didn't hear anything about that, except, naturally, for seeing him after the end of war. After the end of war he came back into town, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this regarding the second occasion you went to Bijeljina: When did you give your statement to the military court in Bijeljina, were you cautioned that you had to speak the truth, something along the lines of your solemn declaration here?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was something similar to what transpired here, except that there was a typist, a court reporter there, recording everything that had been said, and there was a Trial Chamber, consisting of three judges.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the defence? This major had an opportunity to put all questions he wished to put to you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, and he took full advantage of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Exhibit D24/3 ter. Oh, yes. I believe this one is under seal, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us: When is the first time that you saw this document?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, I saw it while preparing for my testimony today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You will see a copy of it now. Please take a look.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the document I saw yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And prior to that, you had never see it, nor did you receive it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions. PRESIDING OFFICER: Cross-examination for the Prosecution. Cross-examined by Mr. Di Fazio:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Arandjic, following the episode, this man Ramusovic continued to work in the municipality, in the town of Bosanski Samac, didn't he, throughout the remainder of April; he was living there?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: What he did concretely is something that I didn't know. What I did know personally is that he continued living and working in the town of Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And he continued doing that through May, June, July, and August?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. To my surprise, he was not immediately arrested after that incident. No proceedings were instituted against him. I personally was disappointed, given the facts of the incident that had happened. But I, as well as my superiors, bore in mind the fact that he had three brothers who held different views on the situation which obtained there then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was part of a group of people located at bridges whom you have described as Muslim and Croat extremists; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: They were members of paramilitary units. These were paramilitary troops, because there were no legitimate -- they were not any -- no, no legitimate military units had been established in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The case is, isn't it, that from your position, he was a member of a group of Muslim and Croat extremists who were armed and carrying out some sort of armed insurrection? That's correct, is it not, according to your position?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I have to go into some detail to clarify this. In the city of Samac proper --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just repeating what you said in evidence, a matter of not more than 10 or 15 minutes ago, as it was translated to me. You said that the bridge was held by Muslim and Croat extremists and they were trying to gain control of the bridge. Now, that, in a nutshell, is your position, is it not?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: It is not that they tried; they did control the bridge, and they controlled the approaches to the bridge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were in control of the bridge, but they were Muslim and Croat extremists, armed and in control of the bridge; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: They were armed civilians, members of the Croatian and Muslim peoples, and probably members of national parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Obviously, paramilitaries, armed paramilitaries, Croatian and Muslim extremists and armed paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, one could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, furthermore, this man Ramusovic escaped on that occasion, didn't he? He escaped with his gun?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Well, he was allowed to escape. Because I'm not a person who would likely kill a fellow citizen. I am not among those who resort to force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly. So the situation had developed whereby an armed Muslim, paramilitary, who had fired upon the JNA, had left the scene with a weapon. That, in a nutshell, is what had happened?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Well, literally speaking, he fled, in the fear of being liquidated, because he was not aware of what my intentions were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the months that followed the 16th and 17th of April, hundreds of Croat and Muslim men were arrested and kept in detention centres in and around Bosanski Samac; that is so, is it not?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm aware of those facts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we have a situation where a Muslim extremist who has fired upon elements of the JNA has escaped with his weapon, hundreds of Croat and Muslim men are being arrested in the months that follow, but what saved this man was the fact that he had some brothers in the 4th Detachment; is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I object to this question. This would speculate what had this man -- it's calling for speculation. Whether it was this or some other reason, he cannot say that. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, as far as you're aware, as far as you're aware, you saw -- you heard the commanders, these leaders in the 4th Detachment, saying words to the effect that he -- trying to cool the matter down and prevent his arrest. That's the immediate reaction you saw upon reporting the matter when you got back to the command of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: When, I've already described this clearly, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what you could see, from what you heard, what saved him was the fact that the commanders of the 4th Detachment, including Simo Zaric, wanted to cool the situation down, and that's what prevented the arrest, until much later?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, again, this is actually the same question, that I already objected about. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were told not to make any report, not to raise the matter, not to publicise the matter, not to heat the matter up, not to pursue the matter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: When I was reporting about this to my superior, I was of the view that I had completed my part of the duty. Whether my superior would opt to further report the incident to other organs and bodies, that was up to the commander, to his assistant, then his deputy. I did not go into that, nor did I investigate their further intentions, so I cannot speak on their behalf on that score now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was apparent to you, was it not -- this is on your own testimony, as I understand it. It was apparent to you that the commanders, including Jovo Savic and Simo Zaric and Radovan Antic, of the 4th Detachment did not wish to publicise the matter, did not wish it to become known generally. That is what I've heard your evidence. That is the situation, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And just one clarification. I mean that we heard very -- very loud and clear from this witness that there was one commander. So when you say "commanders," there is only one commander. The others were assistants -- MR. DI FAZIO: High-ranking officers, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: -- deputies -- MR. DI FAZIO: High-ranking officers. I don't want to get bogged down in that sort of detail. High-ranking officers, okay?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was their position, and it was known to you, was it not?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: The assistants were not higher-ranking officers in relation to me. They were in fact reserve, non-commissioned officers, whereas I was a reserve officer. So an assistant commander can be a reserve, non-commissioned officer, if there are no officers available.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're not getting anywhere here, Mr. Arandjic. My question is really very, very simple. It's simplicity itself. When you got back and you spoke to Jovo Savic, Simo Zaric, Radovan Antic, it was clear that they did not wish you to publicise the matter or make it clear -- make it known generally in the community; that is clear, is it not? This is how I understand your evidence.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: It was up to the commander to decide what he would do next.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you if it's up to the commander to decide what would happen next. I'm just asking you a very simple question. They made their attitude plain: They didn't want the matter publicised or made known. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: I assume that they wanted the matter to be left alone for a while, and that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you went along, months later, or the 40-odd days later, to Milos Savic and reported the matter at the police station, did you make any effort to consult with Simo Zaric or Jovo Savic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That's not what he testified. I apologise. He said that he was called, not that he went there and reported. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, certainly. Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were called --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Inaudible]. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were called, when you were called to the police station, and Milos Savic was there and made it clear to you that he wanted to speak about this matter, did you make any effort to decline to speak to him or try and get in touch with these officers - Zaric, Savic, or Antic - and speak to them about the matter before you made any statements?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: I believed that I did not have to ask for permission to disclose a particular fact to the investigating or law enforcement organs, that is, the MUP. I didn't consult them, because the matter was already well-known to all members of the 4th Detachment. So I didn't consult them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. The matter had become known to all -- many members in the 4th Detachment in the time leading up to his arrest. Did members of the 4th Detachment do anything to arrest him or have him placed in custody of the police, report the matter to the police? Are you aware of any move on the part of 4th Detachment members to bring this man to justice?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that, that anything was undertaken by the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So therefore, it must have been his brothers who protected him, is that your position, the fact of their membership of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Speculation. Speculation.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: I really don't know that. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you worked in the Ministry of Defence just prior to the events of April 16th and 17th and that you worked there with Bozo Ninkovic.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Milos Bogdanovic also worked, I believe, in the Ministry of Defence around that time. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, the late Milos Bogdanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. He was later -- went off and performed military duties and was killed in action, I believe.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: He was killed in an action, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was a fairly high-ranking man, wasn't he, in the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: He was secretary of the Municipal Secretariat for National Defence of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the period of time following the 16th and 17th of April, was he, Milos Bogdanovic, a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: I think he was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Bozo Ninkovic? Was he a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Bozo Ninkovic, I'm not quite sure when, but he took up duty as head of a department of the Defence Ministry in the course of 1992, as it was called then. I think he was a member of the Crisis Staff, but what duties he performed, I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You touched upon the events of the 16th and 17th of April, and you said that you heard shooting during the night of the 16th and 17th of April, and in the morning you went -- you were called to your command and you were informed of the latest developments. Who informed you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Of course, my commander, of course, Radovan Antic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course, Simo Zaric was there, because he was commander of security affairs, and of course, given the events of the night, that must have been a matter that was directly and entirely within his province of responsibility -- END OF RECORDING.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: -- for speculation. All right. I'm okay with the question whether Mr. Zaric was there, but the rest of this question, it's just speculation, whether -- MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric was there, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: He was, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was briefing you on the events of the night and how the situation had developed?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe the witness already said that he was informed by the commander, so -- MR. DI FAZIO: No. This is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: -- it's not fair to the witness. He has said: I was informed by a commander. And now you're putting to him that it was Mr. Zaric who informed him. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, I'm perfectly entitled to do so, and I'll persist with the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Zaric inform you of the developments of the night, what had happened, what was happening?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: The commander Savic -- or rather, the commander Radovan Antic was duty-bound to inform me, as an inferior, and the others who had responded to the call, about the newly development situation. Zaric was present, but of course it is always the commander in such cases who has the main say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Zaric, therefore, had as good an opportunity as you did to be informed of the latest developments that had taken place during the night and in the early morning?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: I don't know to what extent this is important for this event, but probably he was informed. I hope he was informed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was -- were you informed of the activities of any Serbian paramilitaries during the night? Was there any report on that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you: Even though I was a company commander, I was not at all informed, because 10 or 15 days prior to these events, the nights were so stressful. We were in expectation of incursions by Croatian forces across the Sava River and the possibility of paramilitary Croatian forces coming from the village of Prud, so that we were all under stress, both I and my family. And since the telephones were not operating, there was a lot of speculation and people didn't know what was going on. It was only after I went to the command that I was informed what had actually happened. PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Di Fazio -- sorry. You have five minutes. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No doubt your time -- the times were stressful, but my question is very simple. When you went to the command that morning, the morning of the 17th, were you briefed on the activities of Serbian paramilitaries in the town during the night?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was informed about them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told to take action against them?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: You see, the situation was highly complex, very complicated, and there were paramilitary formations active on the Serbian, Muslim, and Croatian sides, so that the 4th Detachment too found itself in this highly complex position. And I've already told you that the 4th Detachment of the JNA was a unit that was still in the process of being formed, and it was still growing. And as I said, that morning a very small number of members arrived, not more than 30 to 40 of them, in response to the call.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told to take action against the Serbian paramilitaries or not? Very simple. You can answer it with a yes or a no.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Our task was, as I already said, to take up defence positions on the west of the town, along the Bosna River, and to protect the town from the incursions by Croatian paramilitary forces from Prud. As for Serbian paramilitary forces, that was not discussed, nor was any particular order issued in connection with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the reason for that, of course, is that you and the 4th Detachment were cooperating with them that night, weren't you, with the Serbian paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: No, that's not true. That is not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about subsequent days? Were you briefed to take any action against Serbian paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: The next few days, the town -- armed individuals were still in presence in town, civilians, members of various paramilitaries, who would sporadically open fire from buildings in the town, and it took several days for those operations to be neutralised, that is, the action being taken from certain buildings, fire being opened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But one thing is absolutely crystal clear: On the 17th of April, the 4th Detachment took action against what you call Croatian and Muslim paramilitaries, but no action against any Serbian paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you that the resistance and the main obstacle to the formation of the JNA 4th Detachment was put up by the SDA and the HDZ, by arming their reserve policemen and their own citizens, civilians, who supported the SDA and HDZ policies. And naturally, it was not to be expected that those Serbian paramilitary forces were not operating against the 4th Detachment; at least, I'm not aware of any such operations by them. PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Di Fazio, your time is up. Do you wish to use some of the minutes left over from this morning? MR. DI FAZIO: No. Thank you very much, Mr. Arandjic. I have no further questions. Re-examined by Mr. Lazarevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Arandjic, you were just answering questions from the Prosecution, and in this re-examination I should just like to go back to a couple of questions for clarification. The Prosecutor asked you, when discussing what the 4th Detachment undertook in connection with your wounding, and you said that more or less everyone knew about it: Did the 4th Detachment do anything to arrest Ramusovic, who had fired at you? And you answered that question. But I'd just like one point of clarification. The 4th Detachment, as a JNA unit, did it have authority to arrest anyone or take anyone into custody?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: No. It had purely military assignments, so that the arrest of Ramusovic, I'm not aware that it was carried out under the patronage of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one more question as a follow-up to this one. Was anyone arrested by the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of it, because there were other MUP bodies who were responsible for security, public law and order, and the rest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Towards the end of your examination by the Prosecution, you were asked a couple of questions in connection with the orders given, that is: Were you ordered to resist the Serbian or any other paramilitary units? I would just like to know, very briefly, what your orders were that day.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: The assignment was very clear and very specific: to take control of the right bank of the Bosna River, to fortify ourselves temporarily for a lying or kneeling position and not allow incursion of Croatian paramilitary forces from the village of Prud, who had tried that night and the following nights to break into the town of Samac, and on that occasion, as far as I know, two members were killed on the very bridge across the Bosna River.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I understand from this you were not told to fight these and not someone else; there were no such orders.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN ARANDJIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Our military assignments were very clear. They always are. They do not have any political nature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if, by any chance, a member of Serbian paramilitary forces, those camouflage people, had opened fire at you, what would you have done? MR. DI FAZIO: Madam Presiding Officer, I do apologise. That is a matter that is rampant -- calls for rampant speculation. PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Lazarevic, are you finished? You are finished? Okay. Mr. Arandjic, thank you very much for coming here today to give your deposition. You may go now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: We'll have the lunch break and we'll start again at 5 past 2.00. Thank you. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.48 p.m.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: Good afternoon, Mr. Erletic. Could you please stand and read the text which is on the pink sheet of paper in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. PRESIDING OFFICER: The Defence for Mr. Zaric. Mr. Pisarevic. Examined by Mr. Pisarevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've already described for you how you should testify. Please do not rush. The interpreters ought to be able to hear you, everything ought to be recorded in the transcript, so please wait until I've asked my question before responding. Please tell us your name and the last name.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Jovan Erletic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you born, Mr. Erletic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 2nd of September, 1951.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I was born in Gornji Zabar, which is now called Pelagicevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us what municipality is that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: That is the municipality of Pelagicevo, formerly belonged to the municipality of Gradacac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where are you residing now?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: At Pelagicevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you complete primary school?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I completed primary school at Gornji Zabar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are you by profession?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I am a caterer by profession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please: Did you do your military service in the Yugoslav People's Army? Where and when?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I served the Yugoslav People's Army in 1971 and 1972, as a member of Tito's Guard, in Valjevo and Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you perhaps hold any military rank?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: My rank is Captain First Class.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell us: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I was married, but I am now happily divorced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What are you by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I am a Serb by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: From the very establishment of the army of Republika Srpska, up to its end, I was a member.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What military duty or officer's duty did you perform as of the 1st of September, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: As of the 1st of September, 1992, I was the operations officer in the technical service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us in what unit and the designation of the unit in which you served.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I was the operations officer on the technical service in the 2nd Posavina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this post that you held imply that you were a member of the command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: My post did not imply that I was a member of the command of the brigade, but as, at the time being, there was no assistant commander for logistics, I performed the duty of assistant commander for logistics, and thereby, and as such, I was a member of the command of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us only where was the headquarters of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: The seat or the headquarters of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade was at Pelagicevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us: In that time period, as of the 1st of September, 1992, who was the commander of the 2nd Posavska Brigade, 2nd Posavska Infantry Brigade, in that period?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: The commander of the 2nd Posavska Infantry Brigade at the time was Lieutenant Colonel Mile Beronja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was the chief of staff of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Captain Milan Josic was the chief of the staff of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know who was the assistant commander for morale, legal, and religious affairs?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: The assistant commander for morale, religious, and legal affairs was Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was the head of the intelligence and security organ in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: The commander of the intelligence and security body in the brigade was Lieutenant Milan Maksimovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you about all the other operations officers, et cetera, but can you tell me: What was the strength of the command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade, in terms of the number of people, of course?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: The command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade numbered 13 members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact -- do you know when, rather, Mr. Simo Zaric assumed the position of assistant commander for morale, legal, and religious affairs in the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the exact date when he assumed that post, but I believe that that was as of the date of the setting up of the 2nd Posavina Brigade, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the command concluded that a memorandum should be drawn up about the practices and incidents that were jeopardising and eroding the morale of the men?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that fact, because I personally took part in that particular assignment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe -- can you tell us approximately in what month did the command arrive at this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, that was in September 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did the command assign -- who did the command charge with the task of preparing this working paper, this working memorandum of that kind?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: As this, in fact, was within the terms of reference of the morale department and the operations officer for morale was Simo Zaric, the commander charged Simo Zaric with performing that particular assignment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what activities Mr. Zaric undertook as part of his terms of reference in order to prepare such a paper?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: We in the command decided, agreed, that this paper should be drawn up as such, and we put Mr. Zaric in charge of it. And as far as I heard, he inspected the units, the companies, the battalions, talked to the men and to their commanding officers, and on the basis of his conversation with them, he prepared these conclusions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did this memorandum, if you remember, of course, when was it discussed in the command of the brigade for the first time?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I believe that that was the end of September 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present when it was being considered, when this memorandum was being considered by the command for the first time?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were all the members of the command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade present?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, they were all present, and that very fact -- because of that very fact, after the reading out of the document and the conclusion of the commander, that was indeed so, as written. We all then affixed our signatures to that document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone else present at that meeting on behalf of the East Bosnia Corps?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Present at this meeting was Lieutenant Colonel Jakovljevic, as, as far as I remember, the security organ in the corps, and Colonel Dosen, as the person in charge of morale in the corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, let us clarify a statement of yours. When you say "When we saw that, we saw that it was indeed so," what exactly did you mean when you said that it was indeed as written, as such? What was the position of the members of the command vis-a-vis that particular piece of information?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: The position of the command was that this information memorandum, had been written well, that we all supported it, upheld what was written in there, and that is why we normally signed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who briefed the people present at that discussion with the content of the information memorandum that was being considered?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: The information memorandum was read out to the present [as interpreted] by the author of the paper, Lieutenant Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the members of the command vote in order to adopt that memorandum?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Since all of us signed the paper after the memorandum had been read out, that in itself was sufficient proof that we had indeed voted in favour of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you well, so you affixed your signatures to it -- you affixed your signature to it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I signed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the other members of the command also sign the document simultaneously?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: After the information memo had been read out, every single man present there signed the paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will Exhibit P127 be shown to the witness, the first and the last page, first and last page, please.
