utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Erletic, please take a look at this document. Is this the information memo that was adopted at a session of the command of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. This is the information memo that was adopted at the meeting of the command of the brigade, and my signature is here under serial number 4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. That was my next question. So all the other people who were present there also signed the document and these are their signatures, to the best of your -- as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: It is true that they signed the document. It is also true that these are their signatures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you remember what happened after the adoption of this memo? Were there any new discussions and meetings in connection with that particular paper; and if so, tell us something about it.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: A couple of days afterwards, after this memorandum had already leaked to the public, there was a meeting organised at the command of the brigade, that is, between members, representatives of the civilian authorities and the command of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, when you say "civilian authorities," who are you referring to? What civilian authorities were there then?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: On behalf of the civilian authorities, the meeting was attended by Mr. Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Stevo Todorovic. The fourth person with them was a man whom I don't know, and I don't know his name, but I do know that they said that he was there on behalf of the MUP or the SUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did this meeting evolve?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: This meeting was a very tumultuous one on both sides, and it ended by the representatives of the civilian authorities walking out on the meeting in protest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall whether at this meeting the commander of the brigade, Beronja, did he preclude this information memorandum from being discussed about by the author of that selfsame paper, Mr. Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can recall that. Yes. I can remember how he forbade him to do so, and individuals, including myself, objected to that, but he said simply: That's the way it is going to be. I'm the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened then with Mr. Simo Zaric, after that? And how did he remain, and on what post, in the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly how much time had elapsed, but I do know that he was later dismissed from that duty and that he ended up as an ordinary soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. Cross-examination. Cross-examined by Mr. Re:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Erletic. My name is David Re. I'm a Prosecutor. I'm going to ask you some questions about the evidence you just gave. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told Mr. Pisarevic that you were a Captain First Class. Is that at the moment or during the war?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: If you understood me well, I had a rank of lieutenant when I served as operations officer for technical service. However, I finished the war with the rank of Captain First Class.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you still hold a rank in the reserve?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Nobody took it away from me, nobody stripped me of it, so I see no reason why I shouldn't have it now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were a member, you said, of Tito's Guard. That is where you did your military service. Between then and the commencement of the war in April 1992, were you in the reserve or did you hold military rank within the army?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: When I left the army, I belonged to the reserve forces of state security detachment in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The state security detachment, that's attached to the state security services, the SDB; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: That's state security service. That's what it was called at the time, before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you, in effect, a reserve officer for intelligence?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I was in reserve forces within the detachment of the state security service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to attain that position, you had to do some military intelligence training, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: That's not correct. I had no training whatsoever. I was simply a member of the reserve forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's a reserve force of the same body that Mr. Zaric was working for for many years, the SDB?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I believe that this is the same force; however, it had nothing to do with me and with where I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long have you known Mr. Zaric for, Mr. Erletic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I've known Mr. Zaric since the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you consider him to be a friend of yours?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: From the very beginning of the war, during the war, and nowadays. I see no reason why he wouldn't be considered my friend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Mr. Tadic? Do you know Mr. Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I don't know Mr. Miroslav Tadic. I've simply heard of him and I saw him a few times in passing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The JNA, in which you did your military service in the 1970s, was one of the largest armies in the world, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: It is not up to me to give assessments, nor do I know the strength of other armies, so I can't tell you whether it was one of the largest or one of the smallest. I can't tell you that, because I don't know much about other armies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The JNA was a very professional army, in your experience in serving in Tito's Guard, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I don't quite understand you. What do you mean, "very professional"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It wasn't a ragtag bag of paramilitaries; it was a professionally highly trained, well-organised, disciplined fighting machine, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: The fact that it was a serious organisation, the army in which I served my military service, that is a correct statement. Now, as to that army being a fighting machinery or whatever you called it, I don't agree with that statement of yours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm asking you about is the discipline within the JNA. I'm asking you whether it was a highly disciplined, professional, well-trained army. If you disagree, just say yes; if you agree with me, agree with me.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: The unit in which I served was the real McCoy; it was the real, professional army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As an officer in the JNA, you received a lot of training in military doctrine, command, and procedures, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: There was the regular procedure, depending on who held which position. That's how it was in the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right. And everyone in the army knew their position and who they reported to. It was part of the training, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's how it was in the army in which I served.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the JNA had tightly controlled structure of command, didn't it, from the bottom right up to the top?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also received training as an officer in the laws of war and the Geneva Conventions, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I have to clarify something here for you. I was a reserve officer, a reserve officer. I was a sergeant in active military. Then once you leave active service, you become a reserve officer. However, I was not an active officer in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you received your training, you received training in the laws of war and the Geneva Conventions, didn't you? It was a standard part of JNA training procedure, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it not true, or you can't remember back 30 years about the lectures you received when you first did your training?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: That's not correct. I can recall it very well. We were not trained to wage war at all. We were not trained to do that. That army was not trained to wage a war. That was an army trained to defend, not to wage a war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were an officer in the VRS for some years, and you are aware that looting is against the laws of war, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: It is unlawful, but I don't know who did the looting. I didn't do it myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Erletic, can you just please concentrate on the question I'm asking you. I didn't ask you who did looting. I'm just talking about looting. Beating of prisoners is also against the laws of war, and you know that from your time as a reserve officer in the JNA and an officer in the VRS; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, let's clarify matters. I was an operations officer for technical service. I had nothing to do with the prison, with the prisoners, with beatings, or anything of that nature. I was neither present nor I was involved in it. I might have heard about that somewhere; however, I did not take part in it. I'm not sure about what other people said. I don't know whether this truly transpired or not. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Erletic, please, I'm not suggesting for a second that you took part in any war crimes. I'm just asking you about your view of war crimes, as a professional officer serving in a professional army. Do you understand that? Just yes or no. Do you understand what I'm saying? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It would be unlawful for a soldier to torture prisoners, wouldn't it? And you can answer that from your training and your experience as an officer in the JNA reserve and in the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I've told you loud and clear that the army and the JNA did not train us to go and fight, or anything of that nature. We were trained to defend our country from aggressors, not to attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you having some difficulty in hearing the question I'm asking and answering the question I'm asking, Mr. Erletic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I have no difficulty understanding your questions or hearing them, but I have a feeling that you're trying to provoke me. I am describing things I know and things where I was present. I can't tell you anything about events where I was not present. I'm no expert at all. I'm an ordinary caterer, and it is not up to me to give assessments on things that had happened. PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Erletic, could you please answer the questions asked by counsel for the Prosecution. It is important for us. It will be important for the Trial Chamber. Counsel for the Prosecution is not trying to imply anything or to trick you into anything; he's just asking simple questions, and it would be very appreciated if you could answer them simply, without arguing with counsel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot give replies to questions to which I don't know an answer or in instances where I'm not an expert. However, I will reply to things that I'm qualified to respond to. PRESIDING OFFICER: If you don't know something, just say so. Just say you don't know, and counsel will move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was: As a long-term officer in the VRS, are you telling us that you don't know whether torture of a prison will be unlawful?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I don't know -- how do you want me to reply to that? With a yes or a no? In this case, I do know the answer. It's yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's very important that you can give us some information to assist the Trial Chamber in its determination of the truth here. I want you to describe the military formation or the units of the -- which were operating at the time of the war breaking out in 1992. There was the 17th Group. The 4th Detachment of the 17th Group of the JNA was in the Bosanski Samac region. What I want you to be -- what I want you to tell the Trial Chamber, when it gets to read and see your evidence, is how the various units were organised in the command and control structure, from the bottom to the top. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you that. I live 30 kilometres from Samac. I am from Pelagicevo. I was operations officer for technical service. As far as logistics is concerned, you can put questions to me, and I did not carry out any other duties and tasks, and I'm not informed about them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already told us, you told Mr. Pisarevic earlier, that you were on the command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade. Was it the entire Posavina Brigade which signed the document which you looked at before?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: If you understood me properly, and I said it clearly, as an operations officer, I did not belong to the brigade command. However, at the time, there was no assistant commander for logistics, so I was acting assistant commander as well, and as such, in that capacity, I belonged to the brigade command. It is true that all 13 members of the brigade had signed that document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question I asked you: Was it the entire brigade command? Is the answer yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As logistics officer, you would have known how many people, how many men, were within the command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many soldiers were there within the 2nd Posavina Brigade command?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean you can't remember now?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I believe we have some slight problems with translation. I have that feeling. I didn't quite follow, because I'm following in B/C/S. Was your question how many members of the command there were or how many soldiers were in the whole brigade, one of these -- in the brigade, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you follow? How many soldiers were under the command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I can't recall that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Hundreds? Thousands?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you that. I don't know exactly. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did the brigade commander, that's Lieutenant Colonel Mile Beronja, report to? Who was his superior officer, or who was that superior officer attached to?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Beronja at the time reported to the East Bosnia Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the East Bosnia Corps the army -- the corps responsible for the Posavina corridor?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I don't know which corridor you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many brigades reported to the East Bosnia Corps?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know how many brigades were within the corps. I don't know that. I don't know. I never looked into that. I was never interested in that and I didn't need to know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a 2nd Posavina Brigade. Was there a 1st and a 3rd and a 4th Posavina Brigade, or rather, Posavina brigades with different numbers?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: There were several brigades, but how many exactly, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they -- each of these brigades had an area, an operating area of responsibility, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the 2nd Posavina Brigade had a distinct geographical area in which it was responsible for all VRS troops, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was responsible for command of all troops within the Samac municipality, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the brigade was broken down into smaller divisions, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the next level down from the brigade? What was the name of the next level or the next division down from the brigade? Was it a battalion or something else?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Well, the next level down from the brigade is a battalion. PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Re, your time is up, but you have eight minutes left from this morning. Do you want to use them?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We have some from tomorrow. Sorry? PRESIDING OFFICER: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I think there are a couple of minutes too for the interruption, which is about two minutes. PRESIDING OFFICER: Okay. So then can you finish in ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you just bear with me for one moment? I understand we can also bank time in advance, same -- we don't -- we go overtime. We don't use it tomorrow. PRESIDING OFFICER: I don't think so, unless the Defence doesn't object, but I mean ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, I will reiterate the position of the Defence, and we are in some kind of preparation for the application for the certification. Because once again, we think that the right of the Defence is to some extent violated, due to the fact that - we have discussed that in The Hague - due to the fact that, for example, if a so-called hostile witness will give testimony here, the other Defence team cannot cross-examine him. And in addition, this practice, with regard to accumulation of time, only for the Prosecution side is also not in accordance with the principle of equality of arms. So, to be brief -- I mean, for the record. I don't want to open any kind of discussions. We cannot accept any such practice with regard to the future time of one side to be collected on this particular day, because otherwise we shall very soon be in some kind of very chaotic or insecure situation in terms of the proceedings. Thank you. PRESIDING OFFICER: I would just want to -- can I respond first? I would just want to note that counsel for the Defence were informed, at a meeting which took place on the Thursday before this week, about the fact that the Prosecution would be allowed to use the time that they didn't use on cross. You didn't attend that meeting, but you were informed of that, I believe, and you would have had time to raise it before the Chamber. But of course, you are free to raise it when you come back. But just for the record, also, because you could have raised it on Thursday afternoon before the Chamber and you could have raised it on Friday before the Chamber. So -- and there was an explanation given at that meeting explaining why the Prosecution would be actually allowed to do that, as opposed to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If I may. We have discussed that in front of the Trial Chamber prior to our trip to Belgrade, so we are very well aware about the instructions, about the position, with that issue, so it's not -- it's not at issue at all. We also proceeded with an oral motion. This motion was denied, overruled. So the only way, in procedural terms, are certification and so on. So we are very well aware about the development with that particular issue. Thank you. DEFENCE COUNSEL: May I just add a few words to what Mr. Pantelic said. The question you addressed to us - at least that is how I understood it - whether unused time -- the Prosecution may use time from the future for this witness. But with regard to this particular topic, we oppose it, we object to it, on behalf of the counsel for Miroslav Tadic, because we were informed by the registrar that they can only use unused time but not time taken in advance. I think that was a clear rule, and we object to any kind of time being used in advance, because I think that would further confuse things, in view of the Rules, which can cause a certain degree of uncertainty, and this would further complicate things. So we oppose any use of time in advance. PRESIDING OFFICER: Actually, when the matter was discussed, I think it wasn't mentioned whether it would be past time or future time. But I agree, in any case, that it creates confusion to use future time, as no one knows if there would be any future time left. And in any case, also, I informed counsel for the Prosecution that we would not count the time for the previous days, that they would only be able to use the time which was left on a given day; otherwise it gets too conflicted and unmanageable. So in accordance with that, you have ten minutes to finish, for now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was asking you about the structure a moment ago, Mr. Erletic. Who did the East Bosnia Corps commander report to? What was the next level of authority?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ultimately, he would have reported to -- he or his superior would have reported to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know that the corps commanders would have reported to either Mladic or someone who reported to Mladic? Are you saying that as an officer, a former officer of the VRS, with Mladic as the officer in charge? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I told you nicely that I was a reserve officer, and I never got involved in these things, nor did they really interest me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object, Madam Presiding Officer, because the Prosecution is asking the witness certain things, though the witness has clearly told him that he was not a trained or professional officer. He's not a military man. If the gentlemen need to know the structure of the army of Republika Srpska, why not call a military expert to whom such questions can be addressed?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I note that objection has taken about a minute and a half of my time. It could have been made in about ten seconds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Erletic, was your evidence that you were a full-time soldier during the war, an officer in the VRS? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether you understood me properly. A professional officer is one thing, and a reserve officer is something quite different. You must make a distinction between a professional soldier and the reserve force. Mr. Prosecutor, I belonged to the reserve force, and I told you that loud and clear from the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a full-time soldier during the war? Yes or no. Simple question. Simple answer, please. Yes or no. Either you were or you weren't.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by "full time." What kind of working hours are you mentioning?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Erletic, your brigade command took some considerable time to consider the document you signed, the 13 of you signed, and I think your evidence said -- was that it was that you signed it after discussions and after Mr. Zaric had reported back to you. Was the document prepared because the brigade command wished to dissociate itself with what the civilian authorities, that is, the Crisis Staff and the War Presidency, were doing with the paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it because the command - sorry - the brigade -- the 2nd Posavina Brigade command was concerned about excessive civilian involvement in military matters?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether anyone feared this or not, but I do know what I personally felt, that is, regarding the arbitrariness of individuals, and we opposed this, and that is what we signed in our -- in that paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you, as a reserve officer in the VRS, concerned about excessive civilian involvement by the Crisis Staff and War Presidency in military matters?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I told you a moment ago: We were against certain cases of arbitrary behaviour and actions taken by individuals who were causing disturbances and who were trying to mistreat anyone, and we wrote that down, loud and clear, and signed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your concern, and that of the other members, or the other people who signed that document, was of civilian, that is, Crisis Staff and War Presidency involvement in the things you've listed there, such as isolation, looting, beating, and enrichment; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: All that is contained in that report is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your concern was about the involvement of the Crisis Staff and War Presidency in all of those things: the beatings, the arrests, the isolations, the looting, and the enrichment of some people?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I told you a moment ago: I personally was concerned, as were the others with me and whom we talked to and agreed on this. Everything that contributed to lowering the morale of the soldiers in the brigade concerned us, and that is why we signed that information memo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were concerned, and the other members of the brigade command were concerned, about the War Presidency and Crisis Staff's discriminatory practices in relation to non-Serbs in the Samac region. Was that one of the reasons why you signed the document?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I told you quite clearly: Anything that contributed, coming from whatever quarter, to the lower morale of the soldiers was something we were concerned about, and we clearly stated in that report what we meant and we signed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Discrimination against non-Serbs by the Crisis Staff, War Presidency, and their practices in discriminating against non-Serbs, one of the reasons that caused you to sign that document?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN ERLETIC
utterances.text: I told you that I was in Pelagicevo. I don't know who committed any discrimination, but we were against that too. PRESIDING OFFICER: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Madam Presiding Officer. PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Erletic, thank you very much for coming to give your deposition today. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: at 3.15 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 6th day of February, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.
